title: Genomics and social practices at Mogou and other Gansu sites during prehistoric trans-Eurasian exchange.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Europe PMC record (paywalled: isOpenAccess=N, inPMC=N, hasSuppl=N, hasTMAccessionNumbers=N, so no full text, no data availability statement, no supplementary tables); Europe PMC text-mined accessions (none); NCBI BioProject search for 'Mogou' (0 hits); NCBI elink from PubMed ID 42691998 to all databases (only the Elsevier full-text link, no repository link); NGDC/CNCB (National Genomics Data Center, China) BIG Search for 'Mogou' (page is JavaScript-rendered and returns no server-side results); ENA (European Nucleotide Archive) study-title search (API returned 404). No data file of any kind was opened.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything substantive: 149 usable individuals from the Mogou cemetery and ten other Gansu sites, 4,700-3,000 years before present; no detectable western/central Eurasian ancestry; no clear matrilocal or patrilocal pattern; no strong evidence of biological relatedness among co-buried individuals; non-local ancestry associated with lower-status burials. A secondary web source states 185 samples sequenced and that data are at ngdc.cncb.ac.cn, but I could not confirm an accession or reach any file.

a1_downloadable.note: No data file reachable. The article is paywalled with no PubMed Central copy and no supplementary files in Europe PMC, so the data availability statement and the archaeological metadata tables (burial, site, date, sex, status) are not retrievable. NCBI BioProject/SRA have nothing for 'Mogou' and PubMed elink gives no repository link. A third-party summary points to NGDC/CNCB (China's National Genomics Data Center) but its search is client-side only, so no accession could be confirmed; Chinese human genome depositions there are frequently under GSA-Human controlled access requiring an application. Also, the primary deposit would be raw sequencing reads, which project rules forbid downloading.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: The interesting labels (burial status, co-burial grouping, local vs non-local ancestry) are archaeological annotations plus model-derived ancestry estimates that would have to be joined from supplementary tables I cannot access, and 'non-local ancestry' is itself an inference, not a measured column.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs would be genome-wide genotypes; none were retrievable. If deposited, they are raw reads (BAM/FASTQ) requiring alignment and pseudo-haploid genotype calling, not an analysis-ready matrix.

a4_units_stated.note: Could not check any file; no units, coverage fields or genotype encodings were observed.

a5_enough_rows.note: 149 individuals passed quality filtering (paper's abstract; a secondary source says 186 sequences from 185 samples). Far below the ~400-row floor for classification. Pairwise framings (149 x 148 / 2 = 10,878 pairs) are non-independent, and the paper reports essentially no close relatives, so the positive class for kinship is near empty.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~1-2 GB if it were an EIGENSTRAT 1240k genotype matrix for 149 individuals
a6_fits_laptop.note: Size is the one thing that would not have been a problem; a 149 x 1.23M pseudo-haploid matrix fits a 16 GB laptop easily. Raw BAMs would not, but they are out of scope anyway.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Already inconsistent before any file was opened: the abstract says 149 individuals, a secondary summary of the same paper says 185 samples / 186 sequences / 11 sites. With no download, there is no way to say which number describes the released data.

a8_label_provenance.note: The headline label, 'non-local ancestry', is the output of the authors' own population-genetic modelling (principal component analysis plus admixture/qpAdm-style fitting) run on the same genotypes that would be the features. Predicting it from those genotypes is circular by construction, exactly the A8 leakage failure.

existing_models.name: KIN, a hidden Markov model for relatedness from low-coverage ancient DNA (Genome Biology 2023)
existing_models.score_and_split: Authors report correct classification of relatives up to 3rd degree from as little as 0.05x genome coverage, evaluated on simulated and published ancient genomes; not a train/test split in the machine-learning sense.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Distinguishing specific relationships of the same degree (e.g. siblings vs half-siblings vs avuncular) and handling contamination remain hard.

existing_models.name: PANE, principal component analysis plus non-negative least squares for ancestry proportions in ancient genotype data (Genome Biology 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported to recover ancestry proportions reliably in simulated admixture scenarios including high missingness; evaluated against qpAdm-style references, not a held-out benchmark.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Reliability when source populations are poorly represented by available reference panels.

existing_models.name: GLIMPSE-based ancient genome imputation pipeline (Nature Communications 2023) and archaic-ancestry inference on imputed ancient genomes (Nature Communications 2026)
existing_models.score_and_split: Imputation accuracy benchmarked by downsampling high-coverage ancient genomes and comparing to the high-coverage truth; archaic-segment calls validated against previously published introgression maps.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Accuracy below ~0.5x coverage and in populations distant from the modern reference panel.

backbone.name: None appropriate. DNA language models (Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT-2, HyenaDNA) embed sequence context, not population-level pseudo-haploid genotype matrices; population genetics here is served by PCA/qpAdm-style statistical models.

integration.partner_dataset: Allen Ancient DNA Resource (AADR), the Reich lab's curated compendium of published ancient human genomes at ~1.23 million SNPs, openly downloadable from Harvard Dataverse
integration.join_key: individual-level genotypes at the 1240k SNP panel, matched on sample ID once these individuals are folded into a future AADR release
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Pooled with AADR one could ask whether burial treatment across many Eurasian cemeteries is predictable from genetic ancestry and relatedness, but that is a project about AADR, not about this paper, and it needs AADR's thousands of individuals rather than these 149.

controls.positive_control: Would have been: recover genetic sex from X/Y coverage, and recover the known east-west Eurasian ancestry axis on principal component 1.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle burial-status labels across individuals and confirm collapse to the majority class.
controls.external_validation: AADR (Allen Ancient DNA Resource) holds thousands of other ancient individuals with site and burial metadata, so an external test set exists in principle.

honest_claim_h3: At best: 'among 149 individuals from eleven Gansu sites, genetic ancestry is associated with burial status' - an association in one region with a sample too small to support a predictive model, and with the ancestry label itself produced by the authors' own modelling of the same genotypes.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use ancient human genome data to predict the social status of a prehistoric burial.
plain_idea.train_on: Genome-wide genotypes of ancient individuals buried in Gansu, China, 4,700-3,000 years ago, plus the archaeological description of each grave. Verified count: 149 individuals (from the abstract); no file was opened.
plain_idea.predict: The burial's status category (rich vs poor grave goods and tomb type), as recorded by the excavating archaeologists; alternatively whether two individuals buried together were biological relatives, as judged by shared DNA segments.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Archaeologists argue about whether social rank in early farming societies tracked ancestry or kinship; a model that predicted status from genomes across many cemeteries would turn that argument into a measurable claim. With 149 individuals from one region it cannot.

more_or_better_data.why: 149 individuals is a rounding error next to the Allen Ancient DNA Resource's thousands of published ancient genomes at 1.23 million SNPs, and KIN and PANE were developed and tested against far larger simulated and published collections.

confidence_score.why: No replicate measurements are accessible and, with 149 individuals spread over eleven sites, most sites would have too few people to estimate per-group uncertainty.

models_beatable.why: KIN (2023), PANE (2025) and the 2023/2026 imputation and archaic-ancestry pipelines are recent, open, and benchmarked by downsampling high-coverage genomes against known truth; they also solve different tasks than social-status prediction, so there is nothing to beat here.

guaranteed_improvement.why: The first condition already fails: no data file could be obtained, so no baseline could be run and no model trained.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: predict burial status (high vs low grave-good category) or co-burial relatedness from genome-wide ancient genotypes of 149 Gansu individuals, with the Allen Ancient DNA Resource as an external test set. Dies on sample size, on label circularity (the 'non-local ancestry' predictor is itself an output of the authors' population-genetic modelling of the same genotypes), and on data access.

effort.compute_note: Not estimated: no data file was obtainable, so there is nothing to size. A 149 x 1.23M genotype matrix would be trivial on a laptop if it existed in reach.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the individuals. The abstract itself gives 149 - under the ~400 floor for a classification task - and that check costs one minute.

verdict_reason: No data file could be reached (paywalled article, no PubMed Central copy, no supplementary files in Europe PMC, no accession in NCBI or confirmable at NGDC/CNCB), so A1 fails. Even granting access, A5 fails decisively at 149 individuals, and A8 fails because the headline label 'non-local ancestry' is the authors' own model output computed from the same genotypes that would be the features. This is a fine archaeology paper and not a machine-learning dataset.
